ubo_and_aml_profiling.statutory_law_governance: Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act 2009, as amended by the Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Amendment Act 2017; Companies Act 1993, as amended by the Companies (Beneficial Ownership Information) Amendment Act 2023; Financial Markets Conduct Act 2013; Sanctions and Anti-Money Laundering Act 2019; United Nations Act 1946; Russia Sanctions Act 2022; and the New Zealand Companies Office Beneficial Ownership Register Directive, requiring UBO disclosure to Government authorities.

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: New Zealand Companies Office, Registrar of Companies, Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.authentication_path: For Hague Apostille Convention states, the notarized original certificate is submitted to the New Zealand Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade for an Apostille and presented directly to the destination authority; for non-member states, the notarized certificate is certified by the New Zealand Department of Internal Affairs and then consular legalized by the destination country embassy or consulate in New Zealand; the Apostille and consular legalization paths are mutually exclusive and must never be chained.

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: New Zealand Companies Office, Registrar of Companies
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.authentication_path: The current certificate of compliance, issued under the Companies Act 1993, is notarized by a New Zealand notary public; for Hague member states, the notarized certificate is apostilled by the New Zealand Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade; for non-Hague states, the notarized certificate is authenticated by the New Zealand Department of Internal Affairs and then legalized by the destination country embassy or consulate; the two authentication routes are parallel and mutually exclusive and cannot be combined.

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.document_name: Board Resolution and Power of Attorney
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: Board of Directors of New Zealand Limited Company, authenticated by a New Zealand Notary Public
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.authentication_path: The original board resolution and power of attorney are notarized by a New Zealand notary; for Hague states, the notarized instrument receives an Apostille from the New Zealand Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade; for non-Hague states, the notarized instrument is processed through the New Zealand Department of Internal Affairs and then the destination state consulate, without Apostille; sequential use of Apostille and consular legalization is expressly prohibited.

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.document_name: Company Constitution and Articles of Association
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: Directors and shareholders of New Zealand Limited Company, registered with the New Zealand Companies Office
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.authentication_path: A certified extract of the constitution is sealed by the company secretary and notarized; for Hague member states, the New Zealand Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade issues an Apostille on the notarized extract; for non-member states, the extract is first authenticated by the New Zealand Department of Internal Affairs and then submitted to the destination country embassy or consulate for legalization; a document must use only one of the two mutually exclusive paths, never both in sequence.

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.document_name: Bank Reference Letter for Corporate Account Opening
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: Registered New Zealand bank subject to the Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act 2009
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.authentication_path: The bank officer signature on the bank reference letter is notarized by a New Zealand notary; for Hague states, the notarized letter is apostilled by the New Zealand Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade; for non-Hague states, the notarized letter is legalized by the destination country consulate after authentication by the New Zealand Department of Internal Affairs; the apostille route and consular legalization route are parallel alternatives and must never be chained.

ubo_and_aml_profiling.pep_and_sanctions_screening_protocols: All UBOs owning 25 percent or more, all directors, all managers, and all authorized signatories must be screened before incorporation against the OFAC Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons List, the United Nations Security Council Consolidated List, the UK Office of Financial Sanctions Implementation consolidated list, the Australian Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade consolidated list, and the New Zealand Sanctions Register administered by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade under the United Nations Act 1946, the Russia Sanctions Act 2022, and the Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act 2009. Politically exposed persons require enhanced due diligence, including source of wealth documentation, senior management approval, and ongoing transaction monitoring. Negative news screening using Dow Jones or World-Check, plus bankruptcy and company director disqualification checks, is mandatory. Screening results must be documented in an AML/CFT compliance file and refreshed within 24 hours before any disbursement.

statutory_name_clearance_protocol.registry_portal_name: New Zealand Companies Register online portal (companies-register.companiesoffice.govt.nz)
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.language_and_transliteration_doctrine: All company names must be in Latin script; English and Maori are acceptable; Chinese characters and non-Roman scripts are rejected unless phonetically transliterated into Latin characters. The four-tier naming doctrine is: (1) the name must not be identical or confusingly similar to an existing registered name or reserved name; (2) the legal suffix Limited or Tapui must appear exactly; (3) restricted or sensitive words require the approval of the Minister of Business, Innovation and Employment, the Financial Markets Authority, or the Reserve Bank of New Zealand; and (4) the name must not be offensive, deceptive, or otherwise contrary to the public interest under the Companies Act 1993.
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.extension_and_rejection_appeal_sop: If the Companies Office refuses name reservation, the applicant must file a formal reconsideration request with the Registrar of Companies within ten working days of the refusal notice, including the refusal reference, a legal memorandum distinguishing the proposed name from each cited existing name, and a certified copy of the company constitution and board resolution. If reconsideration is denied, the applicant may seek judicial review in the High Court under the High Court Rules 2016 and must simultaneously file a priority-preserving extension application together with three alternative names, because a name reservation that expires cannot be indefinitely renewed.

national_tax_registration_infrastructure.competent_tax_authority: Inland Revenue Department (Te Tari Taake), New Zealand; online taxpayer portal: myIR (https://www.ird.govt.nz/myir/)
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.tax_id_procurement_sop: Step 1: Incorporate the New Zealand limited company under the Companies Act 1993 with the New Zealand Companies Office and obtain the NZ Companies Register number. Step 2: Obtain or confirm the automatic IRD number issued by the Inland Revenue Department for the incorporated company; if no automatic issuance, apply for a company IRD number through the myIR portal using the company's incorporation particulars and New Zealand registered office details. Step 3: Register for GST through myIR once the entity carries on a taxable activity in New Zealand and has, or is expected to have, taxable supply turnover above the NZ$60,000 threshold in a 12-month period, or choose voluntary registration if the threshold is not met. Step 4: For foreign non-resident entities without NZ incorporation that become liable for NZ income tax or GST, apply for an IRD number through Inland Revenue's non-resident company registration process in myIR and supply the same identification, director/shareholder, registered office, and tax residency details required by the Tax Administration Act 1994. Step 5: For NZ_LTD, the IRD number serves as the single tax identification number for income tax, GST, employer obligations, and all liable tax returns; no separate VAT registration number exists.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.statutory_election_mechanisms: None in the US check-the-box sense; New Zealand does not provide an entity classification election. A qualifying closely held company may elect look-through company (LTC) treatment under subpart HB of the Income Tax Act 2007, and GST group registration is available under the Goods and Services Tax Act 1985, but neither is a general hybrid or check-the-box election. Hybrid and branch mismatch rules operate automatically under the Income Tax Act 2007 rather than by election.

indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.statutory_registration_threshold_local_c: NZ$60,000 of taxable supplies in any 12-month period; registration is mandatory once the entity carries on a taxable activity and has, or can reasonably be expected to have, taxable supplies exceeding the threshold within 12 months.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.electronic_invoicing_and_clearance_manda: No real-time fiscal clearance, no tax authority digital stamping, and no mandatory e-invoicing regime. E-invoicing through the Peppol network is voluntary. GST tax invoices must satisfy the content and retention rules in the Goods and Services Tax Act 1985 and Tax Administration Act 1994; a supplier must issue a tax invoice no later than 28 days after a recipient requests it, and all invoices and export evidence must be retained for at least seven years.

export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.zero_rating_eligibility: Zero-rating is available under section 11 of the Goods and Services Tax Act 1985 for goods that are physically exported from New Zealand by the supplier in the course of a taxable activity, and for qualifying cross-border services supplied to a non-resident who is outside New Zealand where the supply is not directly in connection with New Zealand land or goods and is consumed overseas. A ghost kitchen operator's domestic New Zealand deliveries to UberEats, DoorDash, or other local consumers remain taxable at 15% GST; zero-rating applies only to genuine export transactions such as branded packaged food products physically shipped abroad, provided the entity retains contemporaneous evidence of export and overseas payment.
mandatory_customs_documentation_bundle: New Zealand Customs Service export entry lodged through the New Zealand Trade Single Window, including the prescribed export declaration and any required permit for controlled goods
Bill of lading, air waybill, or equivalent official carrier transport document evidencing that the goods left New Zealand
Commercial tax invoice and packing list reflecting the export sale and the zero-rated treatment

Overseas payment evidence such as SWIFT credit advice, foreign currency bank statement, or similar banking record showing settlement from outside New Zealand; note that an Indian-style Inward Remittance Certificate (FIRC) has no statutory status under New Zealand law and is not required
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.audit_scrutiny_and_clawback_penalties: Inland Revenue may audit export supplies and will claw back the 15% GST output tax if the supplier cannot substantiate actual exportation or if the recipient or benefit was in New Zealand. A shortfall penalty under the Tax Administration Act 1994 applies for incorrect tax positions, ranging up to 150% of the tax shortfall for evasion plus use-of-money interest, and deliberate fraud can attract criminal prosecution. The standard four-year reassessment time bar may be extended in cases of fraud or tax evasion, exposing older uncontested zero-rating claims to retrospective adjustment.

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.central_bank_authority: Reserve Bank of New Zealand (RBNZ) - Te Pūtea Matua
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: New Zealand operates a fully floating currency regime under the Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act 2021. The New Zealand dollar is freely convertible on both current and capital account; there are no exchange controls, no surrender requirements, no mandatory approval mechanisms, and no separate foreign exchange administration licensing for ordinary trade or investment flows. Monetary policy and exchange rate stability are managed through inflation targeting and occasional market intervention only in exceptional circumstances. For a New Zealand limited company receiving offshore equity or shareholder loans, the funds can be credited directly to a New Zealand bank account in NZD or hard currencies without prior central bank clearance. New Zealand is an IMF Article VIII jurisdiction, so restrictions on payments and transfers for current international transactions are prohibited. Repatriation of dividends, technical royalties, and management fees is generally unrestricted, but must satisfy the Companies Act distribution rules using a solvency test and tax withholding obligations under the Income Tax Act 2007 and relevant double tax treaties. The principal compliance friction is not FX control, but the anti-money laundering and countering financing of terrorism requirements of the Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act 2009, which oblige reporting entities to verify the origin of funds and beneficial ownership. Reporting entities are also supervised by the Department of Internal Affairs and the Financial Markets Authority for suspicious transaction reporting. Therefore, for treasury structuring purposes, the jurisdiction is a fully open capital account environment where cash can enter and exit through ordinary banking channels with standard SWIFT documentation.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: There is no mandatory export proceeds surrender or conversion regime in New Zealand. Exporters are not required to repatriate foreign exchange receipts within any statutory timeline and are not required to convert a compulsory ratio into New Zealand dollars. The company may retain export receipts in foreign currency in any approved bank account, either onshore or offshore. For tax and accounting purposes, foreign currency revenue is recognized in NZD under the functional currency rules of the Income Tax Act 2007 using an applicable exchange rate at transaction date or year-end. Banking practice for ghost kitchen revenues from UberEats and DoorDash is to treat delivery platform settlements as ordinary commercial trade payments; if the credits exceed reporting thresholds, the bank will require external invoices, merchant statements, and a clear audit trail, but there is no central bank conversion certificate requirement.

tier1_domestic_commercial_banks.account_class: Capital Escrow Account / Basic Operational Currency Account
Basic Operational Currency Account with Multi-Currency Capability
Capital Escrow Account / Basic Operational Currency Account

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: Offshore digital EMIs are partially viable but not a substitute for a registered New Zealand bank account. Under the Banking (Prudential Supervision) Act 1989, only registered banks may accept public demand deposits and provide direct settlement in the Exchange Settlement Account System (ESAS) operated by the RBNZ. Fintech entities such as Airwallex, Wise, and Revolut Business can legally support cross-border payment aggregation and FX conversion for a cloud kitchen if they operate in partnership with a licensed New Zealand bank or hold relevant money in a safeguarded trust structure. However, they cannot issue a simultaneously guaranteed NZD bank account number backed by the Crown's depositor protection regime, and their account structures are not eligible for full corporate lending or credit product integration. Therefore, the prudent treasury design is to establish the primary operating and inward capital account at a Tier-1 domestic bank and use an EMI only as an auxiliary collection rail for high-frequency, low-value marketplace payouts. The legal constraint is not a blanket prohibition, but a functional limitation: EMIs cannot offer statutory deposit insurance, cannot clear through ESAS, and should not be used for escrow, dividend payment, or regulatory capital verification.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: New Zealand AML/CFT law does not impose a mandatory physical branch interview for all corporate account openings, provided the customer due diligence can be completed through equivalent electronic identity verification under the Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act 2009 and the associated AML/CFT rules. In practice, for a non-resident-owned limited company with remote directors, major banks will usually require a certified director identity verification, a brief video interview with the beneficial owners or statutory directors, and confirmation of control over the Companies Office portal. Remote opening through a consular officer is not commonly accepted as a standard corporate banking protocol because consular attestation does not satisfy the bank's independent verification of live identity. A New Zealand resident director or an accredited AML/CFT compliance representative will materially accelerate onboarding. Given a ghost kitchen is delivery-only and may have no customer-facing premises, the bank may further request the entity's commercial premises lease, utility bill, and operational evidence to establish substance.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Beneficial ownership opacity caused by virtual brand owners being concealed under franchise agreements and delivery platform intermediated revenue flows.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Provide a complete group structure chart, a recent Companies Office full company extract listing shareholders, the statutory register of beneficial ownership, copies of all virtual brand licence or ghost kitchen franchise agreements, a written mandate from each ultimate beneficial owner, and a source-of-funds declaration detailing the origin of all initial capital now being credited.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: High-frequency, high-volume microbatch settlement from delivery platforms which can be mischaracterised as trade-based money laundering or layering.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Submit a 12-month merchant settlement statement from UberEats and DoorDash, signed delivery vendor service agreements, brand-level invoice registers, platform payout reconciliation reports, underlying customer voucher or refund logs, and a clear accounting map from platform gross settlement to net bankable proceeds.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Offshore capital injection from a related entity in a low-tax jurisdiction that may raise conduit or round-tripping concerns under the corporate bank’s red-flag policy.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Present the executed share subscription agreement or shareholder loan agreement, SWIFT reference fields identifying the payment as equity contribution or shareholder advance, the remitting company’s audited financial statements, a source-of-wealth letter, a tax adviser memorandum confirming arm’s-length pricing, and proof that no PEP or sanctioned individual controls the remitter.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Higher adverse-media and remote-director risk where the statutory directors are non-resident and have no physical presence in New Zealand, creating uncertainty about the true controller’s profile.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Compile valid biometric passports for all directors and beneficial owners, independent PEP screening reports, UN, OFAC, EU, and Australia DFAT sanctions clearance reports, police clearance or judicial record letters, notarised declarations confirming no adverse media matters, and a registered office service agreement proving physical access in New Zealand.

cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.inbound_capital_injection_routing: The compliant routing is to open a dedicated capital influx account at the chosen Tier-1 New Zealand bank, usually denominated in NZD or USD. The inbound wire should be sent via SWIFT MT103 or MT202 with the beneficiary account reference indicating the correct shareholder or borrower entity. Because New Zealand imposes no foreign exchange purpose-code regime, the remitter should insert a clear commercial purpose in field 70 or 77B such as Equity Investment, Share Capital Contribution, or Shareholder Loan. The receiving bank will apply standard customer due diligence and may request the share subscription agreement, board resolution, loan agreement, and a letter of direction from the non-resident parent entity. There is no statutory capital verifier; the directors will pass a solvency test before issuing shares and later file a return of allotment with the Companies Office. For shareholder loans, thin capitalisation rules must be monitored for interest deductions under the Income Tax Act 2007, and the inbound credit should never settle into an EMI before the registered bank account has received the primary funds.
cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.outbound_trade_disbursements: Outbound trade settlements for ghost kitchen equipment, cloud infrastructure, food packaging suppliers, and cross-border marketing fees can be cleared through standard SWIFT MT103 telegraphic transfers for straightforward payments, with the NZD leg settling via RBNZ's Exchange Settlement Account System when counterparties are domestic. For high-value imported kitchen equipment or foreign franchise technology purchases, a Commercial Letter of Credit issued by the Tier-1 bank gives the beneficiary a reliable independent undertaking and protects against supplier performance risk. Documentary Collections, either documents against payment or documents against acceptance, are permitted and may reduce cost when the trading counterparty is well known and the transaction is low risk. Because there are no exchange control approvals, offshore disbursements are allowed freely, but each payment must reference the underlying invoice, purchase order, or licence contract so that the bank’s transaction monitoring unit can verify the economic substance under the AML/CFT Act. No central bank permit is required for profit remittance, trademark royalties, or repayment of shareholder debt; however, applicable non-resident withholding tax should be deducted at source where required by treaty.
permissible_fx_hedging_instruments: Deliverable FX forwards between NZD, USD, AUD, EUR, and SGD up to 12 months, documented under an ISDA or master foreign exchange agreement with a registered New Zealand bank.
Vanilla foreign exchange options, including puts and calls, to hedge downside exposure on USD or AUD-denominated UberEats and DoorDash settlement balances.
Cross-currency swaps used to match shareholder loan or equipment financing obligations in NZD versus settlement currencies, provided the hedge corresponds to verified cash-flow exposure.
Non-deliverable forwards only for currencies outside New Zealand with convertibility restrictions, because NZD is a freely deliverable currency and NDFs are unnecessary for domestic hedging.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Annual Return (AR30) under the Companies Act 1993
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: New Zealand Companies Office, Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within 20 working days after the anniversary date of incorporation
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: No automatic monetary late fee; registrar issues a compliance reminder, and continued non-filing exposes the company to removal from the Companies Register under section 318 of the Companies Act 1993. Restoration from strike-off requires a court or registrar order plus reinstatement costs.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Inland Revenue Department, New Zealand Government
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: By 7 July for a standard 31 March balance date; non-standard balance dates follow the Inland Revenue due-date schedule for the approved balance date
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late filing penalty of NZD 250 per return; continued non-filing may attract escalation penalties and a default assessment, plus late payment penalties of 1% immediately and 1.5% monthly on unpaid tax.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Audited Annual Financial Statements (mandatory only for large companies under the Financial Reporting Act 2013)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Registrar of Companies via the New Zealand Companies Register
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Due with the annual return filing cycle for the applicable balance date; earlier deadlines apply for FMC reporting entities under the Financial Markets Conduct Act 2013
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Directors may be liable to infringement fees and monetary penalties; continuing failure to file audited financial statements can lead to criminal liability and personal fines of up to NZD 10,000 per offending director plus daily penalties while the default continues.

statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.compulsory_audit_thresholds: A company is classified as large, and therefore cannot rely on audit exemptions, if it satisfies at least two of the following three tests at the end of the income year: total assets exceeding NZD 60 million; total revenue exceeding NZD 30 million; 100 or more full-time equivalent employees. Smaller private companies are exempt from a mandatory statutory audit unless required by shareholders or a third-party contract.
statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.governing_accounting_framework: New Zealand Generally Accepted Accounting Practice (NZ GAAP). Publicly accountable for-profit entities apply Tier 1 NZ IFRS; other for-profit entities may apply Tier 2 NZ IFRS Reduced Disclosure Regime, or Tier 3/4 standards issued by the External Reporting Board for smaller entities.

corporate_registers_and_ubo_annual_confi.ubo_annual_confirmation_protocol: New Zealand does not maintain a separate annual UBO declaration. The annual return functions as the statutory confirmation mechanism and must state the current registered office, address for service, directors, and shareholder details as at the anniversary date. Share transfers registered in the company’s share book during the year are reflected in the updated annual return, and any allotment of shares must be separately notified to the Companies Office within 10 working days of allotment.

recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.registered_office_or_agent_market_range_: USD 150–500 per annum for a New Zealand registered office and company secretarial agency service
recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.statutory_audit_estimated_fee_usd: USD 5,000–12,000 for a Tier 2 statutory audit, subject to transaction volume, payroll scale, and ghost-kitchen delivery revenue complexity

corporate_income_tax_regime.effective_tax_rate_incentives: No general statutory tax holidays exist. Preferential relief includes a 15% refundable R&D tax credit on eligible expenditure, immediate deduction for low-value plant and fittings, and depreciation on kitchen equipment. Tax losses are carried forward for the protocol-assumed limit of 5 years (statutory continuity rules under s IA 5 of the Income Tax Act 2007 may permit indefinite carry-forward subject to 49% shareholder continuity).

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: IR4 (Company/Corporate Income Tax Return) filed electronically through the Inland Revenue 'myIR' secure e-filing portal; paper returns are generally not accepted for companies.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: For a standard 31 March balance date, the IR4 is due by 7 July of the same income year. For non-standard balance dates, the return is due by the 7th day of the 4th month after the company's balance date. Provisional tax for a standard balance date is payable in three instalments: 28 August, 15 January, and 7 May.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Registered company name, New Zealand IRD number, fiscal balance date, and tax agent code.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Enter the NZ IRD number for the NZ Ltd entity; non-resident directors do not alter the company's NZ tax identity but must be disclosed in the director schedule.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: All gross income derived from ghost-kitchen and virtual-brand food sales, including proceeds from UberEats, DoorDash, other aggregator payouts, and any direct delivery sales.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Report only New Zealand-source income. Undertake a sourcing analysis for delivery charges, platform commissions, and customer refunds; ensure all settlement statements are included and reconciled.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Cost of food and packaging, delivery-commission deductions, rent, utilities, kitchen staff wages, depreciation, equipment leases, insurance, and administrative expenses.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Claim only expenses incurred in producing NZ assessable income. Keep platform commission statements and supplier invoices; disallow any expenditure not sufficiently evidence-backed.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Accounting profit computed under NZ generally accepted accounting practice before income tax adjustments.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Reconcile directly to underlying management accounts and platform settlement reports. Any unreconciled reconciling items will attract audit scrutiny.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Add non-deductible expenditure (entertainment, non-deductible interest under interest limitation rules, fines or penalties) and deduct non-taxable income or additional deprecation claims.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Apply thin-capitalisation and transfer-pricing adjustments for transactions with the foreign parent or associated entities; amend for any apportionment of NZ-source income.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Adjusted taxable income after applying all deductions and adjustments, being the base for the 28% corporate tax rate.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Where treaty relief applies, first compute full NZ taxable income, then claim credits and reduced withholding at the appropriate lines.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Provisional tax already paid, RWT bank income, non-resident withholding tax credits, imputation credits, and any R&D tax credits.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Attach the IR290 certificate of residence if treaty relief is claimed; attach a schedule of foreign tax credits and withholding certificates for royalties or interest paid to the non-resident.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Late filing: NZ$250 initially, plus NZ$250 per month, capped at NZ$1,000. Late payment: 1% of unpaid tax immediately, an additional 1% after seven days, then 1% each month (or part-month). Shortfall penalties: 20% for lack of reasonable care, 40% for gross carelessness, and 100% for fraudulent evasion.

profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.statutory_dividend_wht_rate: 30% statutory non-resident withholding tax on gross dividends; DTA-reduced rates commonly apply (e.g., 15% for portfolio dividends and 5% for a substantial corporate shareholding requiring at least 10% voting power held for 12 months).
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.treaty_relief_application_protocol: The non-resident beneficial owner must provide the New Zealand paying company with an IR290 'Certificate of Residence' issued by their jurisdiction of residence before the payment is made. The NZ payer retains the certificate and withholds at the DTA-reduced rate. For retrospective claims, the non-resident must file an IR3NP return or amend through myIR, attaching the foreign tax-residence certificate and supporting beneficial-ownership evidence. The NZ company must also report dividends, interest, and royalties in the appropriate return schedules and keep all certificates for six years.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.cross_border_royalty_and_interest_wht: Royalties: 15% statutory NRWT, treaty rates commonly 5%–10%. Interest: 15% NRWT; alternatively, an Approved Issuer Levy (AIL) of 2% may apply if the borrower elects to pay the levy and the interest is paid to a non-resident lender not carrying on business in New Zealand; DTA interest rates often range from 0% to 15%.

transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.tp_documentation_threshold_local_currenc: Controlled transactions exceeding NZ$10 million in aggregate require contemporaneous Local File and Master File-equivalent documentation. Country-by-Country Reporting (CbCR) is mandatory for multinational groups with consolidated group revenue of NZ$1 billion or more.
transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.economic_substance_doctrine: New Zealand does not administer a separate Economic Substance Regulations code like certain offshore centres, but the general anti-avoidance rule (s GA 1 of the Income Tax Act 2007) and transfer pricing rules require genuine commercial substance. A ghost-kitchen NZ company must maintain real operational assets (cooking equipment, rented kitchen premises, staff, platform contracts) and substantive management decisions in New Zealand; otherwise, tax advantages may be denied as a sham or as treaty abuse.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Omitting or under-reporting UberEats and DoorDash settlement payouts, failing to report cash side-deliveries, or using an undisclosed offshore payment account to divert ghost-kitchen revenue.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Shortfall penalty of 100% of the evaded tax, use-of-money interest from the original due date, and criminal conviction under s 144A of the Tax Administration Act 1994, carrying imprisonment of up to five years and fines of up to NZ$25,000 per offence.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who knowingly direct or authorise suppression of income face personal liability for the tax loss, civil restitution orders, departure restrictions (travel bans), disqualification as company directors, and imprisonment.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Shell Company / Lack of Economic Substance
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Operating NZ Ltd as a shell with no physical kitchen, no employees, no kitchen equipment, and no real decision-making, while channelling royalties or delivery income to a foreign parent solely to obtain treaty benefits on dividends or interest.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Invokes the general anti-avoidance rule (s GA 1), recharacterisation of the arrangement, denial of the claimed tax benefit, 100% shortfall penalty, and interest; treaty benefits may be stripped under anti-abuse provisions in the applicable double-tax agreement.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Courts may pierce the corporate veil, rendering directors jointly and severally liable for the company's unpaid tax, with asset-restraint orders, travel bans, disqualification as directors, and civil restitution obligations.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Transfer Pricing Documentation and Arm's Length Failure
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Charging non-arm's-length brand royalty, franchise, or central-kitchen management fees from associated foreign entities without preparing transfer pricing documentation or exceeding the NZ$10 million controlled-transaction threshold without Local File/Master File records.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Transfer-pricing adjustment to the arm's-length amount, shortfall penalties of 20% (lack of reasonable care) to 40% (gross carelessness), interest on underpaid tax, and a NZ$20,000 fine per offence for CbCR non-compliance.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who participate in or conceal mispricing may be personally assessed, disqualified, subjected to asset-seizure orders, held liable for civil restitution, and prohibited from leaving New Zealand.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Failing to implement and maintain an AML/CFT programme when receiving and settling recurring electronic food-delivery payouts, failing to conduct customer due diligence on corporate delivery partners, or failing to submit suspicious-transaction reports.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: The Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act 2009 imposes civil fines of up to NZ$1 million per infringement on an individual and up to NZ$5 million on a business; criminal liability for knowingly involved persons may include imprisonment.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors are individually liable for fines of up to NZ$50,000 per offence; persistent non-compliance triggers personal disqualification, travel bans, asset forfeiture and civil penalties.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Non-Resident Withholding Tax Evasion on Repatriation
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Distributing dividends, royalties, or interest to the foreign parent without withholding NRWT, or applying a DTA-reduced rate without possessing an IR290 certificate of residence for the recipient.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Unpaid NRWT assessed at the statutory 30% dividend rate or 15% interest/royalty rate; late payment penalties, monthly incremental interest of up to 1% per month, and a 40%–100% shortfall penalty for deliberate concealment.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors authoring distributions with knowledge of unpaid NRWT and insufficient imputation credits are personally liable for the tax; directors may also be subject to travel bans, director disqualification, asset restraints, and criminal prosecution.
